title: The Trail of Tears: The Removal of the Choctaw, Chickasaw and Cherokee
traveller: The Choctaw, Chickasaw and Cherokee nations
intro: The United States government, with state militias, forcibly removed the Cherokee from their homeland in the south-eastern United States to Indian Territory, in modern Oklahoma, after the Treaty of New Echota of 1835. Principal Chief John Ross did not sign that treaty and most Cherokee opposed it. The Choctaw and Chickasaw removals are given here as shorter legs; the Muscogee (Creek) and Seminole removals were forced west as well, but the route of neither is told stop by stop.
ending: The removed Cherokee initially settled near Tahlequah. About 4,000 Cherokee died on the trek to Oklahoma, and most deaths were caused by disease, malnutrition and exposure. Some Cherokee evaded removal, and the Eastern Band of the Cherokee Nation descends from those who stayed in North Carolina.

stops.text: The first Choctaw groups met here and at Vicksburg, where a harsh winter brought flash floods, sleet and snow. Alexis de Tocqueville witnessed the removal at Memphis in 1831 and described the Choctaw as tranquil but sombre.
stops.quote: The first groups met at Memphis and Vicksburg, where a harsh winter battered the emigrants with flash floods, sleet, and snow.

stops.text: The Memphis group travelled about 60 miles up the Arkansas to this place. It stayed below freezing for almost a week and ice clogged the rivers, so they could not travel for weeks. Daily rations were a handful of boiled corn, one turnip and two cups of heated water.
stops.quote: The Memphis group traveled up the Arkansas for about 60 miles (100 km) to Arkansas Post.

stops.text: Forty government wagons carried the Choctaw from Arkansas Post to Little Rock. On reaching it, a Choctaw chief called their trek a trail of tears and death. Nearly 17,000 Choctaws made the move, and about 2,500 to 6,000 died.
stops.quote: When they reached Little Rock, a Choctaw chief referred to their trek as a "trail of tears and death".

stops.text: The first Chickasaw group, led by John M. Millard, gathered here with its belongings, livestock and slaves. It crossed the Mississippi and followed routes the Choctaw and Creek had used. In Indian Territory the Chickasaw merged with the Choctaw nation.
stops.quote: The Chickasaws gathered at Memphis on July 4, 1837, with all of their assets—belongings, livestock, and slaves.

stops.text: Martin Van Buren allowed an armed force of 7,000 militiamen, army regulars and volunteers under General Winfield Scott to relocate about 13,000 Cherokees to Cleveland, Tennessee. The Cherokee were held in camps in eastern Tennessee, and their former lands were immediately opened to settlement.
stops.quote: Van Buren allowed Georgia, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Alabama an armed force of 7,000 militiamen, army regulars, and volunteers under General Winfield Scott to relocate about 13,000 Cherokees to Cleveland, Tennessee.

stops.text: The march of 1,000 miles began at Red Clay, the last Eastern capital of the Cherokee Nation. Most walked with scant clothing and without shoes or moccasins. Because of disease they were not allowed into towns or villages and often had to go far around them.
stops.quote: The march began in Red Clay, Tennessee, the location of the last Eastern capital of the Cherokee Nation.

stops.text: After crossing Tennessee and Kentucky, the Cherokee were forced to shelter under this bluff on the Kentucky side of the Ohio River while they waited to cross. Many died huddled together there.
stops.quote: were forced to take shelter under "Mantle Rock", a shelter bluff on the Kentucky side, until "Berry had nothing better to do". Many died huddled together at Mantle Rock waiting to cross.

stops.text: The starving Cherokee reached the Ohio River across from Golconda about 3 December 1838. Berry's Ferry charged them a dollar a head, against its usual twelve cents, and they were not allowed to cross until it had served everyone else.
stops.quote: they arrived at the Ohio River across from Golconda in southern Illinois about the 3rd of December 1838.

stops.text: Several Cherokee were murdered by locals. The Cherokee filed a lawsuit through the courthouse in Vienna, suing the government for $35 a head to bury them. Crossing the 60 miles to the Mississippi took almost three months, and most Cherokee deaths came in southern Illinois.
stops.quote: The Cherokee filed a lawsuit against the U.S. Government through the courthouse in Vienna, suing the government for $35 a head

stops.text: The removed Cherokee initially settled near Tahlequah in Indian Territory. Major Ridge had said on signing the Treaty of New Echota that he had signed his death warrant, and Major Ridge, John Ridge and Elias Boudinot were killed.
stops.quote: Removed Cherokees initially settled near Tahlequah, Oklahoma.

notes: Cherokee dates: the article gives 17 May 1838 for Scott's Order No. 25 and a 23 May 1838 deadline, but ties no stop to them; Cleveland, Mantle Rock, Vienna and Tahlequah are undated. Vienna's lawsuit is not dated; the article's Illinois crossing also mentions a camp 'in Mississippi swamp 4 miles from the river' (letter of 26 December, year unstated), left out as no town is named. Article does not say how removal reached Cleveland vs Red Clay beyond its order; the round-up camps and forts are not named beyond 'camps in eastern Tennessee'. Choctaw Memphis year 1831 from Tocqueville's witness; first-phase groups said to start November 1831. Muscogee and Seminole routes are not given stop by stop, so said in intro. Death figures: Cherokee approx. 4,000 (article); Gilio-Whitaker 'upward of 25 percent'; Choctaw 2,500-6,000 of nearly 17,000. Ending's Eastern Band claim from the article's North Carolina paragraph. Tahlequah text refers to Treaty of New Echota in 1835 per article; killings follow 'resulting political turmoil'. Memphis entry: places.tsv's only Memphis is in Egypt, left null.
